title: Phase Stability and Microstructural Evolution of CaO (5%)-Stabilized Zirconia Top Coatings on 304 Stainless Steel by Atmospheric Plasma Spraying and Laser Cladding
content: Enhancements in the properties of ceramic coatings over time are often driven by the processing techniques. Both thermal spraying and laser cladding are methods used to deposit zirconia coatings, however their mechanisms are differ fundamentally in terms of energy input, coating formation, and bonding to the substrate. In the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) process, the feedstock material is injected as powder particles into high-temperature environment generated by the plasma arc. The heated particles are then accelerated and propelled by a gas jet toward the substrate. Laser cladding is a surface modification process in which a high-energy laser beam is used to melt both the coating material and a thin surface layer of the substrate. The high temperatures involved can induce phase transformations. The phase transformation of Zirconia (ZrO2) from the tetragonal to monoclinic phases is accompanied by a large shear strain and volume increase of approximately 3-5% upon cooling from high temperature, which can lead to residual stresses [1-3]. The reversible transformation of the monoclinic to the tetragonal phase within the temperature range of 950-1170 oC causes microcracks that can propogate and evolve into macrocracks [3, 4]. These phase transformations typically lead to cracking, which contributes to the failure of the thermal barrier coating (TBC) system. The presence of stabilizers, such as CaO-stabilized ZrO2, play a crucial role in phase stability. The microstructure development of metal oxides-stabilized ZrO2 coatings on stainless steel substrates depends on both the processing technique conditions and the characteristics of the injected powders. This study investigates the phase composition and microstructure of CaO (5%)-stabilized ZrO2 coatings on 304 stainless steel substrates produced by APS and laser cladding.
